'''Baddesley Clinton''' is a [[moat]]ed [[manor house]], about 8 miles (13 km) north-west of the town of [[Warwick]], in the village of [[Baddesley Clinton (village)|Baddesley Clinton]], Warwickshire, England. The house probably originated in the 13th century, when large areas of the [[Forest of Arden]] were cleared for farmland. The site is a [[Scheduled Ancient Monument]]<ref>{{National Heritage List for England|num=1013155|desc=Baddesley Clinton Hall moated site and fishponds|access-date=18 June 2020}}</ref> and the house is a [[Grade I listed building]].<ref>{{National Heritage List for England|num=1035136|desc=Baddesley Clinton House and bridge over moat|grade=I|access-date=20 August 2014|fewer-links=yes}}</ref> The house, park and gardens are owned by the [[National Trust]] and open to the public; they lie in a [[civil parish]] of the same name.

==History==
The history of Baddesley Clinton begins with a saxon named Badde, although spelling is variable, who sheltered cattle in a clearing in the wood known as a leah or ley. From this, we have Badde's Ley.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Baddesley Clinton’s history {{!}} Warwickshire |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/warwickshire/baddesley-clinton/the-history-of-baddesley-clinton |access-date=2026-05-14 |website=National Trust |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260514161511/https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/warwickshire/baddesley-clinton/the-history-of-baddesley-clinton |archive-date=2026-05-14}}</ref> 

After the [[Norman Conquest]] beginning in 1066, Baddesley was granted to Geoffrey de Wirce. Next it was transferred to Walter de Bisege and remained with his family until his great-granddaughter Mazera inherited the property and it became the property of the Clinton family through her marriage to Sir Thomas Clinton in 1290. This is when the estate became known as Baddesley Clinton.<ref>''ibid.'' National Trust.</ref>

[[File:Baddesley Clinton house south west 2016.jpg|thumb|Baddesley Clinton rear (south-west) elevation]]
In 1438, John Brome, Under-Treasurer of [[Kingdom of England|England]], purchased the [[Manorialism|manor]], which passed to his son, Nicholas Brome (d.1517), who rebuilt the nearby [[parish church]] dedicated to St Michael, as a [[penance]] for having murdered the parish priest, a crime reputed to have been committed inside the house. The house from this period was equipped with gun-ports, and possibly a [[drawbridge]] over the moat. When Nicholas Brome died in 1517, the house passed to his daughter, who in 1500 had married Sir Edward Ferrers, [[High Sheriff of Warwickshire|Sheriff of Warwickshire]]. 

[[Henry Ferrers (antiquary)|Henry Ferrers]] (1549–1633), "The Antiquary", believed to have built the [[great hall]], made many additions to Baddesley Clinton, including starting the tradition of installing [[stained glass]] to represent the family's [[coat of arms]]. Such glass survives in many rooms. In the 18th century the great hall was rebuilt in brick and the east range was extended, though with great care to continue the style of the original building.
 
[[File:Baddesley Clinton 2017 045.jpg|thumb|left|Interior of Baddesley Clinton]]
The house was inhabited in the 1860s by the novelists [[Georgiana Chatterton]] and her second husband [[Edward Heneage Dering]], who both converted to Roman Catholicism.<ref>ODNB entry on Chatterton, Henrietta Georgiana Marcia Lascelles. [http://www.oxforddnb.com/view/article/5187 Retrieved 13 November 2012. Pay-walled].</ref> The house's [[Catholic]] chapel was rebuilt, and the house was generally refurbished. Major interior changes took place up until the 1940s, with the first floor outside the chapel being completely altered. The interior comprises a great hall, parlour and library, with other rooms, and contains much 16th century carving and furniture and 19th century accessories used by later inhabitants. The house is surrounded by extensive formal gardens and ponds. Many of the farm buildings were built in the 18th century.

The house remained in the Ferrers family until 1940, when it was purchased by Thomas Walker, a relative of the family who changed his name to Ferrers. His son, who inherited it in 1970, sold the estate in 1980 to the [[National Trust]], which now manages it.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Baddesley Clinton: The story of a house |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/baddesley-clinton/features/baddesley-clinton-the-story-of-a-house |access-date=2020-06-18 |website=National Trust |language=en}}</ref>

==Relationship with Catholicism==
[[File:Baddesley Clinton 2017 110.jpg|thumb|Baddesley Clinton]]
The Ferrers appear to have remained [[Roman Catholic]] [[recusancy|recusants]] after the [[Protestant Reformation|Reformation]], along with many other members of the [[Warwickshire]] [[gentry]]. They sheltered Catholic priests, who were under threat of a death sentence if discovered, and made special arrangements to hide and protect them. Several [[priest holes]] were built, secret passages to hide people in the event of a search by the authorities. One such priest hole is in the roof and is reputed to hold six people. A second is hidden in an old privy. Fugitives were able to slide down a rope from the first floor through the old [[garderobe]] shaft into the house's  sewers, which run the length of the building, which could hold six or seven people with their clothes and the equipment required for a Mass. These priest holes are said to have been built by [[Saint Nicholas Owen]], a lay-brother of the [[Jesuit]]s who constructed many masterful hides, notably at nearby [[Harvington Hall]]. He was eventually caught and tortured to death by the [[Protestant]] English government. A third space off the Moat Room, is simply a small room with a door hidden in the [[wood panelling]] and there is no real evidence that this is a hide. 

The priest holes came into use at least once, in 1591 when a conference of Jesuit priests was raided by local authorities. The search is described in the Autobiography of Fr John Gerard, who was hiding during the search. The hides proved effective as no-one was caught.<ref>{{cite web |title=The raid on Baddesley Clinton remembered |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/features/the-raid-on-baddesley-clinton-remembered |access-date=30 October 2017 |publisher=National Trust |language=en}}</ref>

== Gardens and parkland ==
[[File:Baddesley Clinton house north-west 2016.jpg|thumb|left|Viewed from the north-west]]
Parkland to the north and south-east of the house is today meadow with scattered trees, and ornamental trees south of the house. Pleasure grounds to the south-west lead down to a small lake. A formal walled garden, used in the past as a kitchen garden, lies to the south of the house; the central courtyard of the house is also laid out as a garden. The park and gardens are designated Grade II on the [[Register of Historic Parks and Gardens of special historic interest in England|Register of Historic Parks and Gardens]].<ref>{{National Heritage List for England|num=1001186|desc=Baddesley Clinton Hall: park and garden|access-date=18 June 2020|fewer-links=yes}}</ref>

==Filming location==
In 1986 a number of exterior and interior shots of Baddesley Clinton were used by [[Granada Television]] for its ''[[Sherlock Holmes (1984 TV series)|Sherlock Holmes]]'' series in the episode "[[The Adventure of the Musgrave Ritual]]". In October 2016 the house was the venue for [[BBC One]]'s ''[[Antiques Roadshow]]''.<ref>{{cite web |title=Baddesley Clinton 1, Series 39, Antiques Roadshow - BBC One |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b07zw2lh |access-date=16 October 2016 |publisher=bbc.co.uk}}</ref>

Although described as "Baddesley Clinton" on the screen, the location used for the outdoor filming of the  first episode of the 2017 [[BBC One]] miniseries ''[[Gunpowder (TV series)|Gunpowder]]'' depicting events surrounding the 1603 [[Main Plot]] raid was not actually Baddesley Clinton, but was [[Fountains Hall]] near [[Ripon]] in Yorkshire.<ref>{{cite web |title=Our places in explosive BBC series Gunpowder |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/features/our-places-in-explosive-bbc-series-gunpowder |access-date=7 November 2017 |publisher=National Trust}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |author=Hordley, Chris |date=20 October 2017 |title=Where is BBC's Gunpowder filmed? |url=http://www.creativeengland.co.uk/story/Where-BBC-Gunpowder-filmed |access-date=7 November 2017 |publisher=Creative England}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |author=Laker, Chris |date=31 October 2017 |title=Where is Gunpowder filmed? |url=http://tv.bt.com/tv/tv-news/where-is-gunpowder-filmed-11364219879206 |access-date=7 November 2017 |work=TV News |publisher=BT}}{{Dead link|date=July 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Pickard |first1=Michael |date=12 October 2017 |title=Gunpowder, treason and plot |url=http://dramaquarterly.com/gunpowder-treason-and-plot/ |access-date=5 November 2017 |website=Drama Quarterly}}</ref>

1289938.title: Penshaw Monument
1289938.extract:
The Penshaw Monument (officially the Earl of Durham's Monument) is a memorial in the style of an ancient Greek temple on Penshaw Hill in the metropolitan borough of the City of Sunderland, North East England. It is located near the village of Penshaw, between the towns of Washington and Houghton-le-Spring in historic County Durham. The monument was built between 1844 and 1845 to commemorate John Lambton, 1st Earl of Durham (1792–1840), Governor-General of British North America and author of the Durham Report on the future governance of the American territories. Owned by the National Trust since 1939, it is a Grade I listed structure.
The monument was designed by John and Benjamin Green and built by Thomas Pratt of Bishopwearmouth using local gritstone at a cost of around £6000; the money was raised by subscription. On 28 August 1844, while it was partially complete, its foundation stone was laid by the 2nd Earl of Zetland in a Masonic ceremony which drew tens of thousands of spectators. Based on the Temple of Hephaestus in Athens, it is a tetrastyle temple of the Doric order, with eighteen columns—seven along its longer sides and four along its shorter ones—and no roof or cella (inner chamber).
One column contains a spiral staircase leading to a parapeted walkway along the entablature. This staircase was closed to the public in 1926 after a 15-year-old boy fell to his death from the top of the monument. The structure fell into disrepair in the 1930s and was fenced off, then repaired in 1939. It has since undergone further restoration, including extensive work in 1979 during which its western side was dismantled. Floodlit at night since 1988, it is often illuminated in different colours to mark special occasions. The National Trust began to offer supervised tours of the walkway in 2011.
Penshaw Monument is a local landmark, visible from up to 80 kilometres (50 mi) away. It appears on the crest of Sunderland A.F.C. and is viewed nationally as a symbol of the North East. It has been praised for the grandeur, simplicity and symbolic significance of its design, especially when seen from a distance. However, critics have said it is poorly constructed and lacks purpose; nineteenth-century architectural journals condemned its lack of a roof and the hollowness of its columns and walls. It features no depiction of the man it honours, and has been widely described as a folly.

'''Charlecote Park''' is a grand 16th-century [[English country house|country house]], surrounded by its own [[Deer park (England)|deer park]], on the banks of the [[River Avon, Warwickshire|River Avon]] in [[Charlecote]] near [[Wellesbourne]], about {{convert|4|mi|km|0}} east of [[Stratford-upon-Avon]] and {{convert|5.5|mi|km|0}} south of [[Warwick]] in [[Warwickshire]], England. It has been administered by the [[National Trust]] since 1946. It is a [[Grade I listed building]]<ref>{{NHLE|num=1381799|desc=Charlecote Park |access-date=24 September 2023}}</ref> and is open to the public. The park and gardens are listed Grade II* in Historic England's [[Register of Parks and Gardens]].<ref>{{NHLE|num=1001187|desc=Charlecote Park |access-date=24 September 2023|fewer-links=y}}</ref>

==History==
The Lucy family owned the land from 1247. Charlecote Park was originally built in 1558 by Sir [[Thomas Lucy]], and Queen [[Elizabeth I]] stayed in the room that is now the drawing room. Although the general outline of the original Elizabethan house remains, the present house is of mostly Victorian construction. Successive generations of the Lucy family modified Charlecote Park over the centuries until George Hammond Lucy ([[High Sheriff of Warwickshire]] in 1831) inherited the house in 1823 and set about recreating the house in its original Tudor style.

Charlecote Park covers {{convert|185|acre|ha|lk=on}}, backing on to the River Avon. [[William Shakespeare]] was said to have [[poaching|poached]] rabbits and deer in the park as a young man, and to have been brought before the magistrates.<ref name="terr">[http://shakespeare.palomar.edu/timeline/lostyears.htm Terry A. Gray, ''The Lost Years'', Palomar College.] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110928004117/http://shakespeare.palomar.edu/timeline/lostyears.htm |date=2011-09-28 }}</ref>

From 1605 to 1640, the house was occupied by Sir [[Thomas Lucy (died 1640)|Thomas Lucy]]. He had twelve children with [[Alice Lucy|Lady Lucy]], who ran the house after he died. She was known for her piety and for distributing alms to the poor each Christmas. Her eldest three sons each inherited the house in turn, then it fell to her grandson Sir Davenport Lucy.<ref>Richard Cust, ‘Lucy, Alice, Lady Lucy (c.1594–1648)’, Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, Oxford University Press, 2004; online edn, January 2008 [http://www.oxforddnb.com/view/article/66713, accessed 25 November 2015]</ref>

High up on one wall in the Tudor great hall is the 1680 painting ''Captain Thomas Lucy'' by Sir [[Godfrey Kneller]], dated 1680.  It includes what is believed to be one of the earliest depictions of an enslaved black presence in the [[West Midlands (region)|West Midlands]]. The painting includes a young black groom in the right hand background, dressed in a blue livery coat and red stockings and wearing a gleaming, metal collar around his neck. The National Trust notes that "It is not known if Kneller painted this unidentified figure from a model or if it is a portrait of a real groom in Captain Lucy's household".<ref>https://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/533847</ref>

In 1735, a black child called Philip Lucy was baptised at Charlecote.<ref name=gruniad>[https://www.theguardian.com/society/2007/mar/21/communities.raceintheuk Beyond the Grave], Alison Benjamin, 21 March 2007, The Guardian, Retrieved 26 November 2015</ref>

The lands immediately adjoining the house were further landscaped by [[Capability Brown]] in about 1760. This resulted in Charlecote becoming a hostelry destination for notable tourists to Stratford from the late-18th to mid-19th century, including [[Washington Irving]] (1818), Sir [[Walter Scott]] (1828) and [[Nathaniel Hawthorne]] (c 1850).{{citation needed|date=May 2020}}

[[File:Lucy Deerskin created by Edith Mary Hinchley nee Mason.png|thumb|upright|The "Lucy Deerskin" created by Edith Mary Hinchley<ref>{{Cite web|last=Trust|first=National|title=Family tree 533596|url=http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object|access-date=2020-11-22|website=www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk|language=en}}{{Dead link|date=June 2021 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>]]
Charlecote was inherited in 1823 by George Hammond Lucy (d. 1845), who in December 1822<ref>{{cite book |title=Mistress of Charlecote: The Memoirs of Mary Elizabeth Lucy 1803-1889. [Victor Gollancz 1983; cited Orion edition 2002] |author=Alice Fairfax-Lucy.}}</ref> had married Mary Elizabeth Williams of [[Bodelwyddan Castle]], Wales, upon whose extensive diaries the current "behind the scenes of Victorian Charlecote" are based. Seven years of major renovation and rebuilding, including an extension on the river side, were commenced in 1829 after a builder's survey had revealed grave defects in the fabric.<ref>{{cite book |title=Mistress of Charlecote: The Memoirs of Mary Elizabeth Lucy 1803-1889. [Victor Gollancz 1983; cited Orion edition 2002] |author=Alice Fairfax-Lucy.}}</ref> G.H.Lucy's second son, Henry, inherited the estate in 1847 from his elder brother. In 1848, Mary Elizabeth Lucy had the "wretched old Anglo-Norman church" in the Park pulled down. A new church, built to her design, was completed and opened in February 1853.<ref>{{cite book |title=Mistress of Charlecote: The Memoirs of Mary Elizabeth Lucy 1803-1889. [Victor Gollancz 1983; cited Orion edition 2002] |author=Alice Fairfax-Lucy.}}</ref>

In 1890, artist [[Edith Mary Hinchley]] worked on a family tree image on deerskin that involved the creation of 500 heraldic shields. She did the work because she was a genealogist and a friend of the family. The "Lucy Deerskin" is still at Charlecote Park. After the deaths of both Mary Elizabeth and Henry in 1890, the house was rented out by Henry's eldest daughter and heiress, Ada Christina (d. 1942). She had married Sir Henry Ramsay-Fairfax, (d. 1944), a line of the [[Fairfax Baronets]], who on marriage assumed the name Fairfax-Lucy.<ref>{{cite book |title=Mistress of Charlecote: The Memoirs of Mary Elizabeth Lucy 1803-1889. [Victor Gollancz 1983; cited Orion edition 2002] |author=Alice Fairfax-Lucy.}}</ref>

From this point onwards, the family began selling off parts of the outlying estate to fund their lifestyle. In 1946, Sir Montgomerie Fairfax-Lucy, who had inherited the residual estate from his mother Ada, presented Charlecote to the National Trust ''in lieu'' of death duties. Sir Montgomerie was succeeded in 1965 by his brother, Sir Brian, whose wife Alice researched the history of Charlecote and assisted the National Trust with the restoration of the house.<ref>{{cite book |title=Mistress of Charlecote: The Memoirs of Mary Elizabeth Lucy 1803-1889. [Victor Gollancz 1983; cited Orion edition 2002] |author=Alice Fairfax-Lucy.}}</ref>

==Today==
The [[Great Hall]] has a barrel-vaulted ceiling made of plaster painted to look like timber and is a fine setting for the splendid collection of family portraits. Other rooms have richly coloured wallpaper, decorated plaster ceilings and wood panelling. There are magnificent pieces of furniture and fine works of art, including a contemporary painting of Queen Elizabeth I. The original two-storey Elizabethan [[gatehouse]] that guards the approach to the house remains unaltered.

On display at the house is an original letter from [[Oliver Cromwell]], dated 1654, summoning then-owner Richard Lucy to the [[Barebone's Parliament]]. Also on display is a 1760 portrait of George Lucy by [[Thomas Gainsborough]], which cost Lucy the sum of eight [[Guinea (British coin)|guineas]].<ref>Malan, A. H., (1899) "Famous Homes of Great Britain and Their Stories"</ref>

A set of archives for the Lucy family at Charlecote is held by the [[Warwickshire County Record Office]].<ref>[http://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/a2a/records.aspx?cat=187-l6&cid=-1#-1 LUCY OF CHARLECOTE at nationalarchives.gov.uk]</ref> The house also has a display of carriages and a period laundry and brew room.

In April 2012, Charlecote Park featured as the venue for [[BBC1]]'s ''[[Antiques Roadshow]]''.

Charlecote Park has extensive grounds. A [[parterre]] has been recreated from the original 1700s plans. The livestock at Charlecote includes fallow deer and Jacob sheep, which were brought to England from Portugal in 1755 by George Lucy.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/charlecote-park/features/explore-the-parkland-this-summer|title=Explore the parkland at Charlecote this summer|last=|first=|date=|website=National Trust|access-date=}}</ref>

1704737.title: Gibside
1704737.extract:
Gibside is an estate in Tyne and Wear, England. It is located in the valley of the River Derwent on the border with County Durham, between Rowlands Gill and Burnopfield. The estate is the surviving part of a Georgian landscaped park, primarily created under the ownership of Sir George Bowes (1701–60) and designed in large part by Stephen Switzer and William Joyce. 
The park contains structures designed by James Paine, including a Palladian chapel; Daniel Garrett, including a banqueting house; and William Newton, but several are now ruined shells or have been demolished. Gibside Hall, the house at the centre of the estate, dates in part from the 17th century, is Grade II* listed, but is also a shell.
Gibside descended by marriage from the mid-13th century, and passed to the Bowes family in 1693. It was sold piecemeal during the 20th century; the banqueting house is now owned by the Landmark Trust, and much of the rest of the estate by the National Trust.

Sir [[George Bowes (MP for County Durham)|George Bowes]] (park) | original_use = | restored = 1965 onward | current_use = | architect = | sculptor = | architecture = | visitors_num = | visitors_year = | visitors_ref = | governing_body = | owner = [[National Trust]], [[Landmark Trust]] | website = [https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/north-east/gibside Official website] | designation1 = Grade II* Listed Building | designation1_offname = Gibside | designation1_date = 1 February 1950 | designation1_number = {{NHLE|num=1299730|short=yes}} | designation2 = National Register of Historic Parks and Gardens | designation2_offname = Gibside | designation2_date = 1 January 1985 | designation2_number = {{NHLE|num=1000508|short=yes}} }} '''Gibside''' is an estate in [[Tyne and Wear]], England. It is located in the valley of the [[River Derwent, North East England|River Derwent]] on the border with [[County Durham]], between [[Rowlands Gill]] and [[Burnopfield]]. The estate is the surviving part of a Georgian [[Landscape architecture|landscaped park]], primarily created under the ownership of Sir [[George Bowes (MP for County Durham)|George Bowes]] (1701–60) and designed in large part by [[Stephen Switzer]] and William Joyce.{{Cite book |last=Roberts |first=Martin |title=County Durham |last2=Pevsner |first2=Nikolaus |author-link2=Nikolaus Pevsner |last3=Williamson |first3=Elizabeth |publisher=Yale University Press |year=2021 |isbn=9780300225044 |edition=3rd |series=The Buildings of England |location=New Haven; London |pages=436–441 |language=en}}{{Cite book |last=Hall |first=Gemma |title=Gibside |publisher=[[The National Trust]] |year=2016 |isbn=9781843594536 |editor-last=Feldman |editor-first=Amy |language=en}} The park contains structures designed by [[James Paine (architect)|James Paine]], including a [[Palladian architecture|Palladian]] chapel; [[Daniel Garrett]], including [[Banqueting House, Gibside|a banqueting house]]; and [[William Newton (architect, 1735–1790)|William Newton]], but several are now ruined shells or have been demolished. Gibside Hall, the house at the centre of the estate, dates in part from the 17th century, is [[Grade II* listed]], but is also a shell. Gibside descended by marriage from the mid-13th century, and passed to the [[Bowes-Lyon family|Bowes family]] in 1693. It was sold piecemeal during the 20th century; the banqueting house is now owned by the [[Landmark Trust]], and much of the rest of the estate by the [[National Trust]].{{Cite web |title=The Banqueting House, Gibside, Newcastle upon Tyne: History |url=https://www.landmarktrust.org.uk/search-and-book/properties/the-banqueting-house-4863/#History |access-date=2024-04-06 |website=[[Landmark Trust]]}} ==History== The [[Blakiston baronets|Blakiston family]] acquired the estate by marriage in about 1540. Sir William Blakiston (1562–1641) replaced the old house with a spacious mansion between 1603 and 1620. Both the Royal ([[James VI and I|James I of England]]) coat of arms and the Blakiston coat of arms are seen over the entrance of the old Hall.{{cite web|url=http://dre.durham.gov.uk/pgDre.aspx?&SEARCH=By+Place&TERM=Rowlands+Gill&ID=DRE7238&PIC=Y|title=Photo c1932 - Royal (James I) Coat of Arms over Blakiston Coat of Arms. Gibside Hall|publisher=Durham County Council |year=2009|access-date=12 November 2011}} The Gibside property came into the possession of the Bowes family in 1713; a result of the marriage in 1693 of Sir William's great-granddaughter, Elizabeth Blakiston, to Sir [[William Bowes (MP for County Durham)|William Bowes]] (1657–1707) of [[Streatlam Castle]], [[County Durham]] (now demolished).{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VikAAAAAQAAJ&q=burke%27s+elizabeth+blakiston+sir+william++bowes+gibside&pg=PA65|title=A Genealogical and Heraldic History of the Extinct and Dormant Baronetcies of England|publisher=Burke's Peerage|access-date=14 October 2012|year=1838}} Until 1722,{{PastScape |mname=Gibside Hall |mnumber=22481 |access-date=26 October 2013}} the basis of the Bowes' influence was their own estate and house of Streatlam Castle. However, after that date the acquisition through marriage of the Blakiston estate of Gibside gave the Bowes family an even greater influence in the north of the county and a share in the immense wealth that was to be acquired from the coal trade. The Blakiston estate included some of the area's richest coal seams.{{cite web|title=Bowes and Strathmores – Gibside and Streatlam |url=http://www.sunnisidelocalhistorysociety.co.uk/bowes.html|publisher=Sunniside Local History Society|access-date=21 October 2012}} In 1767 the granddaughter of Sir William Bowes – the "Bowes heiress" [[Mary Eleanor Bowes]] – married [[John Bowes, 9th Earl of Strathmore and Kinghorne|John Lyon, 9th Earl of Strathmore and Kinghorne]], who changed his surname to Bowes due to a provision in her father's will that any suitor had to take the family name. This was a device to continue the Bowes lineage in the absence of a male heir.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZABSepHO1FMC&pg=PA515|title=The British Chronicles|volume= 2|page=515|first= David |last=Hughes|year=2007|publisher=Heritage Books|isbn=978-0788444913}} After the split inheritance dispute following the death of [[John Bowes, 10th Earl of Strathmore and Kinghorne]], in 1820, it belonged to his legitimated son [[John Bowes (art collector)|John Bowes]] until his death in 1885 (he is buried in the Gibside chapel), when under the [[entail]] it reverted to his cousin [[Claude Bowes-Lyon, 13th Earl of Strathmore and Kinghorne]]. It had been the main residence of John Bowes' mother, Mary Milner, by then Dowager Countess of Strathmore, and her second husband, the politician Sir [[William Hutt (politician)|William Hutt]] (who had been John Bowes' tutor), and remained in his ownership until his death in 1882.{{cite web|url=https://archivesearch.lib.cam.ac.uk/repositories/2/archival_objects/508369|title=Letter from William Hutt, Gibside Hall, Northumberland|date=22 January 1865|publisher=Cambridge University|access-date=4 September 2022}} ==Park structures== Improvements to Gibside carried out by the [[Bowes-Lyon]] family in the 18th and early 19th centuries included landscaping, Gibside Chapel, built between 1760 and 1812, the [[Banqueting House, Gibside|Banqueting House]], a column of [[Liberty (goddess)|Liberty]], a substantial stable block, an avenue of oaks and several hundred acres of forest. The top floor of the main house was remodelled as a giant [[parapet]] in 1805.{{cite web |title=Gibside Hall |url=https://www.heritagegateway.org.uk/Gateway/Results_Single.aspx?uid=22481&resourceID=19191 |access-date=4 September 2022 |publisher=Heritage Gateway}} ===Chapel=== [[File:Gibside Chapel exterior pic 1.JPG|thumb|The north-east façade of the chapel]] The chapel is located at the south-western end of the Avenue and was begun in July 1760 to a design derived from [[Palladio]] by [[James Paine (architect)|James Paine]]; an unrealised circular design was commissioned in 1737 from either [[Sir Thomas Robinson, 1st Baronet]] or Daniel Garrett. Sir George Bowes died in September 1760, and the shell of the building was completed in 1769 under the supervision of his widow, Mary Gilbert. His grandson [[John Bowes, 10th Earl of Strathmore and Kinghorne]], completed the interior work and had the chapel consecrated in 1812. Sir George was then buried in the mausoleum beneath the building.{{Cite book |last=Roberts |first=Martin |title=County Durham |last2=Pevsner |first2=Nikolaus |author-link2=Nikolaus Pevsner |last3=Williamson |first3=Elizabeth |publisher=Yale University Press |year=2021 |isbn=9780300225044 |edition=3rd |series=The Buildings of England |location=New Haven; London |pages=436–441 |language=en}}{{Cite book |last=Hall |first=Gemma |title=Gibside |publisher=[[The National Trust]] |year=2016 |isbn=9781843594536 |editor-last=Feldman |editor-first=Amy |language=en}} The building was designed in the [[Palladian architecture|Palladian]] style and takes the form of a [[Greek cross]] within a square, with a dome on a drum over the crossing. The north-east facade, which faces the Avenue, is the most highly-decorated part of the building. It consists of a double [[portico]], the inner order consisting of six unfluted [[Ionic columns]] and the outer of four, carrying the pediment. The two outer columns on each side of the inner portico are engaged, the gaps between them being filled by arched openings. The whole facade is topped by six urns. The other three facades are plainer, and feature [[Diocletian window|Diocletian windows]] in the end elevations of the cross arms. Internally, the arms of the cross are [[apse]]d and [[groin vault]]ed and the crossing and corners are domed. The [[entablature]] and arches are richly decorated, as intended by Paine, but the rest of his decorative scheme, which would have included [[Coffer|coffering]] in the apses and dome and statues in the niches of the apses, was not carried out. Nevertheless, the nineteenth-century cherrywood furnishings are of high quality and complete. They consist of a [[Holy Table|holy table]] surrounded by rails; a triple-decker [[pulpit]], the [[sounding board]] supported by a single Ionic column; and [[Box pew|box pews]] in the corners and side apses, the latter curved to fit the space. The Bowes-Lyons used a box pew in a corner which had underfloor heating. There is a house for the minister nearby. Some holders of the position would not have been able to hold a [[Church of England]] parish living, on account of their views.{{cite web |title=Gibside Chapel |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/gibside/features/celebrate-gibside-chapel |access-date=4 September 2022 |publisher=National Trust}} ===Orangery=== The orangery was built between 1772 and 1774 for [[Mary Eleanor Bowes]], who had a keen interest in botany, to a design by [[William Newton (architect, 1735–1790)|William Newton]]. The building has a seven-bay arcade of [[Tuscan column|Tuscan columns]] to the front and plain three-bay arcades to each side, the rear arch on each side filled with a pedimented doorway, which lead into lobbies. The rear contains five sash windows, the middle three forming a canted bay with views across the Derwent valley. The building, which originally had a slate roof, was converted into a conservatory by [[John Bowes (art collector)|John Bowes]] in 1885 by the addition of a glazed iron roof; at the same time a brick podium was constructed in the centre of the main room to display plants and a heating system added, with a boiler installed in the western lobby. The roof was removed between the First and Second World Wars, since when the orangery has been a roofless shell, however the fabric was consolidated by the National Trust in 2005. ===Stables=== The stables were built between 1746 and 1751. The design was probably by Daniel Garrett, and is similar to his Fenham Hall in Newcastle-upon-Tyne. The building forms a quadrangle around a courtyard, with the main entrance in the south wing and an exit in the west wing, thus enabling carriages to pass through without needing to turn. The east wing, which contained the visitor entrance and which faced the new coach drive created for Sir George, is decorated in the Palladian style. The centre projects in a five-bay block, with a pediment over the central three bays. The door occupies the centre bay of the ground floor, and is flanked by niches and set within a three-bay blind arcade, and there are two [[Aedicula|aedicules]] in the outer bays. The first floor has five sash windows. Inside, some plasterwork and the stalls of the show stable survive, the latter separated by narrow wooden classical columns. ===Banqueting House=== {{Main articles|Banqueting House, Gibside}} The [[Banqueting House, Gibside|Banqueting House]] was built in 1746, and is an early example of [[Gothic Revival architecture]], of the early form often called "Gothick". It has now been restored and is available for letting by the [[Landmark Trust]], who now own it.{{cite web |title=Landmark Trust website: the Banqueting House |url=http://bookings.landmarktrust.org.uk/BuildingDetails/Overview/133/The_Banqueting_House# |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110623133130/http://bookings.landmarktrust.org.uk/BuildingDetails/Overview/133/The_Banqueting_House |archive-date=23 June 2011 |access-date=20 May 2011}} ===Column to Liberty=== [[File:Gibside Estate Monument - geograph.org.uk - 240856.jpg|thumb|The Column to Liberty]] The Column to Liberty was built between 1750 and 1759 to a design by Garrett, but completed by Paine after the former's death in 1753. It consists of a pedestal bearing a [[Roman Doric]] column, which at {{Convert|42.7|m|ft|abbr=on}} was, when constructed, the second-tallest column monument in England after the [[Monument to the Great Fire of London]]. The column is topped by a statue of a woman, personifying Liberty and originally gilded, who holds the Staff of Maintenance and [[Cap of Liberty]]. It represents George Bowes' support for the [[Whig Party (British political party)|Whig Party]]. ==Later history== The Bowes-Lyon family had other major country houses, [[Glamis Castle]] in Scotland, and [[Streatlam Castle]], [[County Durham]],{{cite web|title=Bowes and Strathmores – Gibside and Streatlam |url=http://www.sunnisidelocalhistorysociety.co.uk/bowes.html|publisher=Sunniside Local History Society|access-date=21 October 2012}} located {{convert|30|miles}} to the south.[[Google Maps]], accessed on 12 March 2026 Streatlam Castle became vacant in the 1920s after the Bowes-Lyon family sold some of its properties to pay [[death duties]]. The building was stripped of its fixtures and fittings, with many of the fireplaces and other items being transferred to Glamis Castle. Parts of the structure were demolished in 1958, including the removal of the roof. What remains is protected by [[Grade II* listed]] building status and included in the [[Heritage at Risk Register]].{{Cite web|url=https://historicengland.org.uk/advice/heritage-at-risk/search-register/list-entry/48161|title=Gibside Hall, B6314, Gibside Estate, Rowlands Gill, Whickham - Gateshead | Historic England|website=historicengland.org.uk}} Parts of the grounds have been designated a [[Site of Special Scientific Interest]], including a forest garden.{{cite web|url= https://forestplans.co.uk/uploads/attachment/302/appendices-24.pdf |title=Gibside: Conservation Area Character Statement |page=12}} The chapel and Long Walk have been in the National Trust's ownership since 1965, and an additional {{convert|354|acre|km2}} of the grounds were acquired in 1993. The Banqueting House has been in the ownership of the [[Landmark Trust]] since 1981, the building having been restored from a derelict shell. The stables now house a learning and discovery centre.{{Cite web|title=Gibside National Trust - Historical attractions in Gateshead|url=https://newcastlegateshead.com/business-directory/things-to-do/gibside-national-trust|access-date=2021-08-04|website=NewcastleGateshead|language=en}} [[Women's Land Army]] girls were billeted at Gibside during World War I.{{NHLE |num=1017224 |desc=Gibside Hall, 17th to 19th century country house|access-date=4 April 2015}} ==Gallery== File:Gibside Banqueting House.jpg|The [[Banqueting House, Gibside|Banqueting House]] File:The Banqueting House, Gibside, side and front view - geograph.org.uk - 514906.jpg|Another view File:Gibside Column to Liberty pic 2 (cropped).JPG|The top of the Column to Liberty, the figure seen from behind File:Gibside Chapel interior 2018 - pulpit.jpg|Centrally-placed three-decker [[pulpit]] at Gibside Chapel, a private chapel on the Calvinist edge of [[Anglicanism]] File:Gibside Chapel interior 2018.jpg|Interior of the chapel File:Gibside Long Walk pic 2.JPG|The Column to Liberty can be seen from the porch of Gibside Chapel File:Gibside Orangerie pic 1.JPG|Shell of the [[orangery]] File:Gibside Stables pic 3.JPG|The stables File:Gibside Stables pic 1.JPG|Side of the stable block ==See also== *[[Grade II* listed buildings in Tyne and Wear]] *[[18th-century Western domes]] ==References== {{reflist|2}} ==External links== {{commons category|Gibside}} *[https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/gibside Gibside information at the National Trust] *[https://3dwarehouse.sketchup.com/model/9d0e2a6927ae4aa4c2b7610c425a01c9/Gibside-Chapel 3D model of Gibside Chapel] {{SSSIs Tyne and Wear}} [[Category:Grade II listed buildings in Tyne and Wear]] [[Category:Country houses in Tyne and Wear]] [[Category:National Trust properties in Tyne and Wear]] [[Category:Sites of Special Scientific Interest in Tyne and Wear]] [[Category:Parks and open spaces in Tyne and Wear]]

1771282.extract:
Souter Lighthouse is a lighthouse located to the North of Whitburn, South Tyneside, England. (It was generally known as Souter Point Lighthouse when in service). Souter Point was the first lighthouse in the world to be actually designed and built specifically to use alternating electric current, the most advanced lighthouse technology of its day. The light was generated by a carbon arc lamp: first lit on 11 January 1871, it was described at the time as 'without doubt one of the most powerful lights in the world'. 
After being decommissioned by Trinity House (the national lighthouse authority) in 1988, Souter Lighthouse was acquired by the National Trust, who now manage it as a visitor attraction with holiday lets.

'''Souter Lighthouse''' is a [[lighthouse]] located to the North of [[Whitburn, Tyne and Wear|Whitburn]], [[South Tyneside]], England.<ref name="NT">{{cite web |title=Souter Lighthouse and the Leas |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/souter-lighthouse-and-the-leas |website=National Trust |access-date=31 October 2022}}</ref><ref name="Visit ST">{{Cite web |title=Souter Lighthouse |url=https://www.visitsouthtyneside.co.uk/article/9049/Souter-Lighthouse |access-date=13 November 2022 |website=Visit South Tyneside |language=en}}</ref> (It was generally known as '''Souter Point Lighthouse''' when in service). Souter Point was the first lighthouse in the world to be actually designed and built specifically to use [[Alternating current|alternating electric current]], the most advanced lighthouse technology of its day. The light was generated by a [[arc lamp|carbon arc lamp]]: first lit on 11 January 1871,<ref name="Douglass1879" /> it was described at the time as 'without doubt one of the most powerful lights in the world'.<ref name="Elliot1875" /><ref>{{Cite rowlett|engne|accessdate=2016-04-26}}</ref> 

After being decommissioned by [[Trinity House]] (the national lighthouse authority) in 1988, Souter Lighthouse was acquired by the [[National Trust]], who now manage it as a visitor attraction with [[holiday let]]s.<ref name="NT" />

==Location==
The lighthouse is located on Lizard Point, but takes its name from Souter Point, which is located a mile to the south.  This was the intended site for the lighthouse, but it was felt that Lizard Point offered better visibility, as the cliffs there are higher, so the lighthouse was built there instead. The Souter Lighthouse name was retained in order to avoid confusion with the then recently built [[Lizard Lighthouse]] in [[Cornwall]].<ref name="Jones" />

Souter Lighthouse is approximately three miles south of the mouth of the [[River Tyne, England|River Tyne]]. Some four miles or so to the north of the mouth of the Tyne is a sister Victorian lighthouse, [[St Mary's Lighthouse]], on [[St Mary's Island, Tyne and Wear|St Mary's Island]]. It has also been decommissioned, and is open to visitors. St Mary's Lighthouse can be seen with the naked eye from the top of Souter Lighthouse.<ref>Personal observation</ref>

==History==
The lighthouse was a much-needed aid to navigation due to the number of wrecks on the dangerous reefs of Whitburn Steel<ref>{{cite news | title = Newcastle Courant | date = 18 June 1869 | pages = 6 | quote = a new lighthouse to be erected on Souter Point...It will erected to prevent wrecks from occurring, if possible, on Whitburn Steel, of which there have been so many complaints within recent years.}}</ref> which lay directly under the water in the surrounding area. In one year alone – 1860 – there were 20 shipwrecks. This contributed to making this coastline the most dangerous in the country, with an average of around 44 shipwrecks per every mile of coastline.{{Cn|date=July 2022}}

===19th century===
==== Construction ====
[[File:062852-Souter Lighthouse South Shields.jpg|thumb|left|The lighthouse {{circa|1900}}.]]
The lighthouse and associated buildings were designed for [[Trinity House]] by their Chief Engineer, [[James Nicholas Douglass|James Douglass]]; its construction was supervised by on-site engineer [[Henry Norris (engineer)|Henry Norris]].<ref>{{cite news | title = Shields Gazette and Daily Telegraph | date = 9 September 1870 | pages = 3 | quote = the works are being pushed rapidly forward under the supervision of Mr H. Norris, the board and resident engineer }}</ref> Alongside the lighthouse tower a number of other buildings were laid out around a quadrangle, including the engine room and boiler house, and five dwellings; all were built of rubble masonry, [[Cement render|rendered]] with [[Portland cement]].<ref name="Douglass1879" /> The contract for building the lighthouse and keepers' cottages was reported in March 1869 as being £8,000<ref>{{cite news | title = Sheffield Daily Telegraph | date = 11 March 1869 | pages = 2 | quote = A new lighthouse and keepers' residence are to erected at Souter Point near, South Shields.  The contract for building has been let for £8,000. }}</ref> and was awarded to the local firm of James Todd,<ref>{{cite journal | title = The Architect and Contract Reporter: A Weekly Illustrated Journal | page = 183 | volume = 1 | quote = The contract for the erection of a new lighthouse and lighthouse-keepers residence at Souter Point, near Sunderland, has been let to Mr. Todd, builder, of South Shields, for £8,000 | date = January–June 1869 }}</ref> after complaints that local builders had not had the opportunity to reply to tender as it had not been advertised locally.<ref>{{cite news | title = Shields Gazette and Daily Telegraph | date = 12 April 1869 | pages = 2 | quote = Some months ago, tenders were advertised for in the Sunderland papers, asking offers for the erection of a lighthouse on Souter Point. Most of the people in Shields hardly ever saw a Sunderland paper in their lives, yet the Shields builders were virtually shut out from competing for a lighthouse within the limits of their own Poor-Law Union, so far as publicity of the fact of tenders being wanted was concerned. Communications were accordingly made from this office on the subject; the advertisement appeared in the Gazette, and a South Shields contractor ultimately got the job. }}</ref>  The foundation stone was ceremonially laid by [[Richard Collinson|Admiral Collinson]]'s sister on 9 June 1869.<ref>{{cite news | title = Shields Gazette and Daily Telegraph | date = 9 June 1869 | pages = 9 | quote = The foundation-stone of the lighthouse at Souter Point was laid yesterday afternoon by Mrs Blain (sister to Admiral Collinson) in the presence of the committee of the Elder Brethren of the Trinity House, London, Admiral Collinson, Captain Nesbitt, Captain Webb, Mr G. N. Douglas[''sic''], engineer to the Corporation, and friends. Robert [''sic''] Norris is the superintendent of the works, and Mr James Todd is the contractor. }}</ref> Building works were completed in 1870, and the lighthouse entered service in January the following year.<ref name="Douglass1879" /> After completing this project Douglass and Norris moved on to the building of [[Hartland Point Lighthouse]] in Devon.

==== Electricity ====
[[File:Souter Lighthouse arc light mechanism.jpg|thumb|right|upright|The original arc lamp assembly, in use from 1871-1914, now on display in the lighthouse visitor centre.]]
[[Carbon arc]] lights for lighthouses were pioneered by [[Frederick Hale Holmes|Professor Frederick Hale Holmes]], with experiments carried out in 1857–60 at [[Trinity Buoy Wharf|Blackwall]] and at [[South Foreland Lighthouse]] (as described in a lecture <ref>{{cite news | title = Newcastle Courant | date = 30 March 1860 | pages = 3 | quote = MAGNETO-ELECTRIC LIGHT FOR LIGHTHOUSES - Professor Faraday, in a lecture delivered at the Royal Institution, says: "By means of a magnet, and of motion, we can get the some kind of electricity as from the battery; and, under the authority of the Trinity House, Professor Holmes has been occupied in introducing the magneto-electric light in the lighthouse at the North [''sic''] Foreland...For the last six months the North [''sic''] Foreland has been shining by means of this electric light beyond all comparison better than its former light. Never for once during six months has it failed in doing its duty }}</ref> by [[Michael Faraday]] at the [[Royal Institution]]).<ref>{{cite book 
  | title = Electricity Supply in the United Kingdom - A Chronology from the beginnings of the Industry to 31 December 1985 
  | publisher = The Electricity Council 
  | orig-year= 1973 
  | year = 1987 
  | edition = 4th
  | page = 15
  | isbn = 0-85188-105-X 
}}</ref> An initial installation at [[Dungeness Lighthouse]] in 1862 had proved problematic, however, with frequent failures of the lamps and machinery; so Trinity House carried out an extensive testing and selection process over five years (including comparisons with oil lights and examination of equipment in Britain and France)<ref>{{cite news 
  | title = Dover Express 
  | date = 22 May 1868 
  | pages = 4 
}}</ref> before finalising its plans for a complete purpose-built electric installation at Souter.<ref name="Douglass1879" />

[[File:Souter Lighthouse generator.jpg|thumb|left|One of the original magneto-electric generators from Souter Lighthouse (now part of 'Making the Modern World' in the [[Science Museum, London]]).]]
The carbon arc lamp at Souter was placed within a lens array consisting of a [[Third order Fresnel lens|third-order]] fixed [[Catadioptric system|catadioptric]] optic surrounded by a revolving assembly of eight vertical condensing-prisms which produced one bright flash every thirty seconds.<ref name="Elliot1875">{{cite book |last1=Elliot |first1=George H. |title=European Light-House Systems |date=1875 |publisher=Lockwood & co. |location=London |pages=120–127 |url=http://access.bl.uk/item/pdf/lsidyv38f8413f |access-date=10 March 2019 |archive-date=29 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201029210746/http://access.bl.uk/item/pdf/lsidyv38f8413f |url-status=dead }}</ref> Its 800,000 [[candle power]] light could be seen for up to 26 miles.<ref name=Jones /> The [[Fresnel lens|optics]] were designed and built by [[James Timmins Chance|James Chance]] in 1870.<ref name="Chance 1902">{{cite book |last1=Chance |first1=James Frederick |title=The Lighthouse Work of Sir James Chance, Baronet |date=1902 |publisher=Smith, Elder & co. |location=London |page=166 |url=https://uslhs.org/sites/default/files/attached-files/The%20Lighthouse%20Work%20of%20Sir%20James%20T.%20Chance.pdf |access-date=24 February 2019}}</ref> 

In addition to the main light a red/white [[sector light]] shone from a window in the tower below the lantern, to highlight hazards to the south in Sunderland Bay (namely Hendon Rock and the White Stones); it was powered using light diverted (through a set of mirrors and lenses) from the landward side of the main arc lamp.<ref>{{cite web|title=Trinity House History page, quoting Newcastle Courant 12 Jan. 1871|url=https://trinityhousehistory.wordpress.com/tag/souter-point/}}</ref>

Electricity for the light was provided by two of Holmes' own [[magneto (power generation)#Lighthouses|magneto]] electric generators for which he took out a series of patents<ref>{{cite book 
  | title = Biographical Dictionary of the History of Technology 
  | publisher = Routledge 
  | year = 1996 
  | page = [https://archive.org/details/isbn_9780415060424/page/606 606] 
  | isbn = 0-415-06042-7 
  | url-access = registration 
  | url = https://archive.org/details/isbn_9780415060424/page/606 
  }}</ref> during those years. In normal operation only one generator was used, but in conditions of poor visibility both were connected to the lamp to provide a brighter light. The generators were driven by one of a pair of [[Joseph Whitworth|J. Whitworth & co.]] 5 [[Nominal horse power|nhp]] '[[Porter-Allen engine|Allen]]' condensing steam engines.<ref name="Douglass1879">{{cite journal |last1=Douglass |first1=James Nicholas |title=The Electric Light applied to Lighthouse Illumination |journal=Minutes of Proceedings of the Institution of Civil Engineers |date=25 March 1879 |volume=LVII |issue=1,639 |pages=82–87}}</ref> (Prior to being installed at Souter, the engines and generators were exhibited by Trinity House at the [[Paris Exposition of 1867]].) The engines were worked alternately: one week on, one week off. Located in the engine-house, they also drove an air-pump to feed the pressure tank of a foghorn.<ref name="Renton2001" /> 

In December 1891 the lighthouse tower was painted with a broad red band, to make it more conspicuous during the day.<ref>[https://www.thegazette.co.uk/London/issue/26237/page/7213 London Gazette, Issue 26237, Page 7213, 29 December 1891.]</ref>

==== Foghorn ====
Holmes also designed a [[Reed pipe|reed]] [[fog signal]] for the new lighthouse, sounded from a separate foghorn house (east of the tower) through a pair of vertical trumpets (angled north-east and south-east, facing out to sea).<ref name="FogSignals1871">{{cite journal |title=Fog Signals |journal=The Nautical Magazine |date=November 1871 |pages=769–770}}</ref><ref>[https://twsitelines.info/SMR/2489 photo c.1900]</ref> It sounded one blast every 45 seconds.<ref name="FogSignals1879" /> Compressed air for the foghorn was piped underground from the engine room, on the other side of the lighthouse, where the air compressor was driven by a common drive shaft from the engines powering the magnetos.<ref name = "Renton2001">{{cite book |last1=Renton |first1=Alan |title=Lost Sounds: The Story of Coast Fog Signals |date=2001 |publisher=Whittles |location=Caithness, Scotland}}</ref> 

A more powerful [[Siren (alarm)|siren]] fog signal replaced the reeds in February 1879;<ref name="FogSignals1879">{{cite journal |title=Fog Signals |journal=Parliamentary Papers, Volume LXIV |date=1 August 1879 |volume=23 |issue=337 |pages=2–4}}</ref> it sounded one blast every minute.<ref>[https://www.thegazette.co.uk/London/issue/24739/page/4214 London Gazette, Issue 24739, Page 4214, 1 July 1879.]</ref> It required an additional and more powerful engine, which was installed in the engine room to drive the compressor for the new signal.<ref name="Douglass1879" />

===20th century===
[[File:Souter Lighthouse lenses.jpg|thumb|right|upright|The current optical apparatus dates from 1914.]]
====Conversion to oil====
In 1914 the pioneering electric light at Souter was replaced with the latest type of [[mantle lamp|incandescent]] oil lamps (i.e. [[Kerosene|paraffin]] vapour burners). At the same time [[Chance Brothers]] provided a new, much larger lens system: a bi-form [[First order Fresnel lens|first-order]] catadioptric revolving optic (a bi-form lens is double-height, containing two lamps, one above the other). At the same time a new lantern was provided, to accommodate the taller optic. Red shades were placed around the lamps, within the lenses, so that the light now flashed red, once every 5 seconds.<ref>{{cite book |title=Index to Notices to Mariners 1919 |date=1920 |publisher=U.S. Navy Hydrographic Office |location=Washington DC |page=456}}</ref> The 1914 optic remains ''in situ'' in the tower; it weighs 4.5 tonnes and floats on 1.5 tonnes of [[Mercury (element)|mercury]].<ref name="NTFeature" />

A separate lamp was used for the fixed red/white sector light, which continued to shine from its window lower down in the tower.{{Cn|date=July 2022}} 

Having removed the two Holmes magneto-electric machines from the engine room, the Corporation of Trinity House presented one to the [[Institution of Electrical Engineers]] in 1915;<ref name="Parsons1940">{{cite book |last1=Parsons |first1=R. H. |title=The Early Days of the Power Station Industry |date=1940 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge |page=2}}</ref> it is now on display at the [[Science Museum, London]].<ref>{{cite web 
  | url = https://collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk/objects/co36517/holmess-electricity-generator-1867-generators-electric 
  | title = Holmes's electricity generator, 1867 
  | access-date= 1 November 2022 
}}</ref>

The fog signal was improved in 1919 when a more powerful siren was installed, sounded through a pair of [[Lord Rayleigh|Rayleigh]] trumpets.<ref>[https://wondersofworldengineering.com/sentinels.html photo]</ref> (These replaced the twin Holmes trumpets formerly employed; the foghorn house was remodelled at the seaward corners to accommodate them).<ref name="Renton2001" /> The siren gave a 4-second blast every minute.<ref name="WWE1937">{{cite journal |title=Sentinels of the Sea |journal=Wonders of World Engineering |date=23 March 1937 |issue=4 |url=https://wondersofworldengineering.com/sentinels.html |access-date=2 November 2022}}</ref> [[Hornsby-Akroyd oil engine|Hornsby oil engines]] were installed to drive the compressors for the new siren.<ref name="Renton2001" />

====Reversion to electricity====
In 1952 the lighthouse was again converted to run on electric power (this time using [[Incandescent light bulb|incandescent lamps]], powered by [[mains electricity]]).<ref name=Jones>{{cite book|last1=Jones|first1=Robin|title=Lighthouses of the North East Coast|date=2014|publisher=Halsgrove|location=Wellington, Somerset|pages=70–73}}</ref> The 4,500W bulbs used for the main light were the largest in the Trinity House service.<ref name="Jackson1975">{{cite book |last1=Jackson |first1=Derrick |title=Lighthouses of England and Wales |date=1975 |publisher=David & Charles |location=Newton Abbott |pages=110–111}}</ref> Should the electricity supply fail, a diesel generator would be engaged (and in the event that it too were to fail, an additional emergency battery lamp would be engaged). The mechanism which turned the lenses continued to be driven by clockwork at this time, until 1983 when it was replaced by a pair of electric motors.<ref>{{cite web|title=Local history society|url=http://www.ndfhs.org/Reports/st_2002_06.html}}</ref> 

[[File:Souterhouse Fog Horn - geograph.org.uk - 1774891.jpg|thumb|right|The foghorn building, looking out to sea.]]
The fog signal was upgraded in 1953: a Stone Chance [[diaphone]] signal was installed and a pair of [[exponential horn]]s replaced the Rayleigh Trumpets on top of the foghorn building.<ref name="Renton2001" /> At the same time the engine room was provided with two new Reavell compressor sets, one driven by an electric motor, the other by a diesel engine. The diaphone produced a five-second blast every 30 seconds in poor weather, and remained in use up until 1988, when the lighthouse was decommissioned.<ref name="Jones" /> 

===Decommissioning===
Souter Lighthouse was decommissioned by Trinity House in 1988,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.chroniclelive.co.uk/news/local-news/ten-interesting-facts-south-shields-1342148|title = Ten interesting facts about South Shields|date = January 2012}}</ref> but continued to serve as a radio navigation beacon up until 1999 when it was finally closed.

== Present day ==
As Souter was never automated, it remains much in its original operational state except for updates during its lifespan to its lantern and electrical apparatus.<ref name="Jones" />

Today the decommissioned Souter lighthouse is owned by the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] and open to the public; the engine room, light tower and keeper's living quarters are all on view. There is also an outdoor play area, Trusty Club and indoor activities to accommodate young visitors. Two of the former lighthouse keepers' cottages are used as National Trust holiday cottages. The lamps, lenses and foghorn remain in working order and are still activated from time to time 'on special occasions'.<ref name="NTFeature">{{cite web |title=The lamp at Souter Lighthouse, a design marvel |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/features/the-lamp-at-souter-lighthouse-a-design-marvel |website=National Trust |access-date=3 November 2022}}</ref>  

In 2011, [[South Tyneside Council]] and the National Trust commissioned artists Joshua Portway and [[Lise Autogena]] to produce an artistic work around the lighthouse.<ref name="SheffieldHallam">{{cite web |title=Foghorn Requiem|url=https://www.shu.ac.uk/art-design-media-research-centre/archive/foghorn-requiem|website=Sheffield Hallam University|access-date=30 November 2025}}</ref><ref name=Allan2>{{cite book|last1=Allan|first1=Jennifer Lucy|title=The Foghorn's Lament|date=2021|publisher=Hachette UK|location=United Kingdom|pages=268-269}}</ref> The result was [[Foghorn Requiem]], a musical composition written by [[Orlando Gough]] for the lighthouse's foghorn, ships’ horns and brass bands.<ref name="BBCReport">{{cite web |title=Foghorn Requiem: Souter Lighthouse hosts sea performance|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-tyne-23015200|website=BBC News|access-date=30 November 2025}}</ref> On 22 June 2013, it was performed at the lighthouse to an audience of thousands, with 65 musicians and over 50 ships taking part.<ref name=Allan1>{{cite book|last1=Allan|first1=Jennifer Lucy|title=The Foghorn's Lament|date=2021|publisher=Hachette UK|location=United Kingdom|pages=1}}</ref>

The Gatehouse is the oldest part of the house and is flanked by later wings, in the Strawberry Hill Gothic style, popularised by Horace Walpole.

'''Coughton Court''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|k|oʊ|t|ən}}<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.coughtoncourt.co.uk/the-house.html |title=The House at Coughtoncourt.co.uk/ |access-date=2010-09-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110623232649/http://www.coughtoncourt.co.uk/the-house.html |archive-date=2011-06-23 |url-status=dead }}</ref>) is an English [[Tudor style architecture|Tudor]] [[country house]], situated on the main road between [[Studley, Warwickshire|Studley]] and [[Alcester]] in [[Warwickshire]]. It is a Grade I [[listed building]].

The house has a long [[battlement|crenellated]] façade directly facing the main road, at the centre of which is the Tudor Gatehouse, dating from after 1536; this has hexagonal turrets and [[oriel window]]s in the [[English Renaissance]] style. The Gatehouse is the oldest part of the house and is flanked by later wings, in the [[Strawberry Hill Gothic]] style, popularised by [[Horace Walpole]].

==History==
The Coughton estate has been owned by the Throckmorton family since 1409. The estate was acquired through marriage to the De Spinney family.<ref name="marshall">Peter Marshall. ''Catholic Gentry in English Society: The Throckmortons of Coughton from Reformation to Emancipation,'' Ashgate Publishing, Ltd., Nov 17, 2009. [https://books.google.com/books?id=0nZErbwRgZIC&q=coughton+court+history ''Google eBook'']</ref> Coughton was rebuilt by Sir [[George Throckmorton]], the first son of Sir Robert Throckmorton of Coughton Court by Catherine Marrow, daughter of William Marrow of London.<ref name="marshall" /> The great gatehouse was dedicated to King [[Henry VIII]] by Throckmorton, a favourite of the King<ref name="marshall" /> who spent most of his life rebuilding Coughton.<ref name="parliament">''The History of Parliament: the House of Commons 1509-1558,'' ed. S.T. Bindoff, 1982. Article: [http://www.historyofparliamentonline.org/volume/1509-1558/member/throckmorton-sir-george-1489-1552 ''THROCKMORTON, Sir George (by 1489-1552), of Coughton, Warws.'']</ref> Throckmorton would become notorious due to his almost fatal involvement in the divorce between King Henry and his first wife [[Catherine of Aragon]].<ref name="marshall" /> He favoured the Queen and was against the [[English Reformation]].  In 1549, when he was planning the windows in the great hall, he asked his son Nicholas to obtain from the heralds the correct [[tricking]] (colour abbreviations) of the arms of his ancestors' wives and his own cousin and niece by marriage Queen [[Catherine Parr]]<ref name="parliament" /> (see gallery drawing). The costly [[recusancy]] (refusal to attend [[Church of England|Anglican Church]] services) of his eldest son, [[Robert Throckmorton (courtier)|Robert]], and his heirs restricted later rebuilding, so that much of the house still stands largely as he left it.<ref name="parliament" />

After Throckmorton's death in 1552, Coughton passed to his eldest son, Robert. The family were practicing [[Roman Catholic|Catholics]] and the house contains a [[priest hole]], although unlikely to be the work of [[Nicholas Owen (Jesuit)|Nicholas Owen]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Hodgetts |first=Michael |title=Secret Hiding Places |edition=2nd |editor=Paul Hodgetts |year=2024 |publisher=Pear Branch |location=Dudley |isbn=9781738427000 |page=30}}</ref>  These were hiding places for priests constructed during the period when Catholics were persecuted by law in England, from the middle of the reign of [[Elizabeth I]]. The Hall also holds a place in English history for its roles in both the [[Throckmorton Plot]] of 1583 to murder Queen Elizabeth, and the [[Gunpowder Plot]] of 1605, although the Throckmorton family were themselves only indirectly implicated in the latter, when some of the Gunpowder conspirators rode directly there after its discovery.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Parishes: Coughton {{!}} British History Online |url=https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/warks/vol3/pp74-86 |access-date=2025-02-07 |website=www.british-history.ac.uk}}</ref>

The house has been in the ownership of the [[National Trust]] since 1946. The family, however, hold a 300-year lease. The family tenant was [[Clare McLaren-Throckmorton]], known professionally as Clare Tritton QC, until she died on 31 October 2017.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://announcements.telegraph.co.uk/deaths/218732/mclaren-throckmorton |title=McLaren-Throckmorton |newspaper=[[The Daily Telegraph]] |author=Guy Tritton |date=22 November 2017 |accessdate=28 November 2017 |archive-date=9 November 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171109081000/http://announcements.telegraph.co.uk/deaths/218732/mclaren-throckmorton |url-status=dead }}</ref> The current residents are Magnus and Imogen Birch Throckmorton.<ref name="Times repairs"/>

The house is open to the public but not all year round. The property is set in extensive grounds including a walled formal garden, a river and a lake. As of 2024, the house is undergoing extensive repairs to the roof and fabric of the building costing £3.3m, with the work set to be completed by June 2025.<ref>{{Cite web |last=McIntyre |first=Alex |date=2024-12-07 |title=National Trust urges Coughton Court visitors to decorate roof tiles |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c93gyq4pxxyo |access-date=2024-12-25 |website=BBC News |language=en-GB}}</ref>

The family managed the property on behalf of the Trust until 2007, when management of the property reverted to the National Trust. The management agreement is renewed every 10 years. The family is due to resume management in 2026. This caused public concern that the family would benefit from money spent by the trust on repair works, with National Trust members no longer able to visit as part of their membership.<ref name="Times repairs">{{Cite web|url=https://www.thetimes.com/uk/society/article/national-trust-coughton-court-throckmorton-family-gxhtgtggv|title=‘Dismay’ as National Trust hands back Tudor manor after £3m repairs|first=Fintan|last=Hogan|date=23 February 2025|website=www.thetimes.com}}</ref><ref name="Independent repairs">{{Cite web|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/travel/news-and-advice/national-trust-coughton-court-throckmorton-family-b2704130.html|title=National Trust members angry as family handed back Tudor house after £3m repairs|date=27 February 2025|website=The Independent}}</ref>

In Autumn 2023 a £3.3 million roof restoration roof project began, scheduled to finish in Summer 2025, with key sections of the roof being restored and structural improvements made to the fabric of the house. The work has been funded by the [[Wolfson Foundation]] and donations from National Trust members and supporters. Phase 4 of the work, over the winter months, was scheduled to fit around the annual migration of the resident bats.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/warwickshire/coughton-court/through-the-roof---coughton-roof-project |title=Through the Roof - FuturepROOFing Coughton |date=21 January 2025 |access-date=21 June 2025}}</ref> Following the restoration National Trust members expressed disappointment over the decision to hand back management of the property to the residing family.<ref name="Independent repairs"/>

==Architecture==

The gatehouse at Coughton was built at the earliest in 1536, as {{Citation span|text=it is built of stones which came from [[Bordesley Abbey]] and [[Evesham Abbey]]|date=December 2024|reason=Listing particulars does not state this}}(both in [[Worcestershire]]) after the [[Suppression of Religious Houses Act 1535|Dissolution of the Monasteries Act]] in 1536. As with other Tudor houses, it was built around a courtyard, with the gatehouse used for deliveries and coaches to travel through to the courtyard.<ref>{{National Heritage List for England|num=1183632|desc=Coughton Court |access-date=25 December 2024}}</ref> Geoffrey Tyack described the gatehouse as a "dazzling monument to family pride, and the angle turrets, large expanses of window and battlemented skyline combine to give an impression of chivalrous splendour".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Tyack |first=Geoffrey |title=The Making of the Warwickshire Country House 1500–1650 |publisher=Warwickshire Local History Society |year=1982 |page=23 |language=en}}</ref> The gatehouse has [[oriel window]]s in the [[English Renaissance]] style and is flanked by later wings, in the [[Strawberry Hill Gothic]] style, popularised by [[Horace Walpole]].{{cn|date=June 2025}} One of the tower turrets contains the priest hole, two secret spaces, one above the other, which were rediscovered in 1858 and still contained a rope-ladder used for access.<ref>[[Michael Hodgetts]] & Paul Hodgetts, ''Secret Hiding Places: Priest Holes: An Incredible True Story of Faith and Ingenuity'' (Pear Branch Press, 2024), p. 31.</ref> The courtyard was enclosed on all four sides until 1780, when the east range opposite the gatehouse was demolished.<ref>{{Cite web |editor-last=Styles |editor-first=Philip |title=Parishes: Coughton in A History of the County of Warwick: Volume 3, Barlichway Hundred |url=https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/warks/vol3/pp74-86 |access-date=2024-12-25 |website=www.british-history.ac.uk |place=London |publication-date=1945 |via=British History Online}}</ref>

After the [[Roman Catholic Relief Act 1829|Roman Catholic Relief Act]] was passed in 1829, the Throckmorton family were able to afford large-scale building works, allowing them to remodel the west front.

== In popular culture ==
The house was used as a filming location for the BBC One series ''[[Father Brown (2013 TV series)|Father Brown]]'' in the episode ''The Mask of the Demon''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt4860336/|title = The Mask of the Demon|website = [[IMDb]]}}</ref>

In June 2025 the restoration of the house's roof was featured in an episode of BBC's series ''Hidden Treasures of the National Trust''. This included the relocation for restoration of the ''Tabula Eliensis'' (1596), a large oil-on-linen painting depicting the history of [[Ely Cathedral]] and the [[coat of arms|coats of arms]] of 29 Catholic noblemen imprisoned by [[Elizabeth I]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/iplayer/episode/m002cg6w/hidden-treasures-of-the-national-trust-series-3-6-raising-the-roof|title=Hidden Treasures of the National Trust - Series 3: 6. Raising the Roof!|via=www.bbc.co.uk}}</ref>

'''Washington Old Hall''' is a historic [[manor house]] in [[Washington, Tyne and Wear]], England. It lies in the centre of Washington, being surrounded by other villages. The building was the ancestral home of the [[Washington family|family]] of [[George Washington]] (1732–1799), the first [[president of the United States]].

==History==
[[File:WASHINGTON OLD HALL INTERIOR, TYNE AND WEAR, ENGLAND.jpg|thumb|left|Interior of the Washington Old Hall|241x241px]]
[[William de Hertburn|William]] de [[Hartburn, County Durham|Hertburne]] (originally William Bayard),<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Wells|first=William C.|date=1913|title=A Washington Token|url=https://www.britnumsoc.org/publications/Digital%20BNJ/pdfs/1913_BNJ_10_21.pdf|journal=British Numismatic Journal|series=2|publisher=British Numismatic Society|volume=10|page=326}}</ref> an ancestor of George Washington, assumed tenancy of the Wessyngtonlands from the [[Bishop of Durham]] in the late 12th century. Soon after, he changed his name to William de Wessyngton (later Washington).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.newcastlegateshead.com/things-to-do/washington-old-hall-p23531|title=Washington Old Hall|publisher=Newcastle Gateshead|access-date=4 April 2015}}</ref> In the early 15th century Sir William Mallory married Dionysia Tempest, the last Wessyngton heir at the Hall.  Dionysia was daughter of Sir William Tempest and his cousin, Eleanor Wessyngton. In 1613, Sir John Mallory (a descendant of Sir William Mallory and Dionysia Tempest) and Anna Eure, shareholders in the [[Virginia Company]], moved south to [[Sulgrave Manor]] in Northamptonshire, and the manor was sold to the Bishop of Durham.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sunderlandecho.com/heritage-and-retro/retro/story-washington-old-halls-thousand-year-history-and-its-american-connection-2905690|title=The story of Washington Old Hall's thousand year history – and its American connection|date=6 July 2020|publisher=Sunderland Echo|access-date=3 December 2020}}</ref>

The Hall continued to be used as a residence until the 19th century, when it became [[tenement]] flats and gradually fell into disrepair. In 1936, the building was declared unfit for human habitation, and was rescued from demolition by Fred Hill, a local teacher, who created what is now the "Friends of the Old Hall" to press for restoration of the building. Restoration began in 1937.<ref>{{NHLE|desc=Washington Old Hall, Sunderland|num=1354971|access-date=3 December 2020}}</ref> Preservation work stopped during [[World War II]], but was completed in 1955. The building was opened by the American Ambassador, [[Winthrop W. Aldrich]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/wear/content/articles/2006/05/23/washington_old_hall_feature.shtml|title=Washington Old Hall|publisher=BBC|access-date=3 December 2020}}</ref> In 1957, the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] assumed responsibility for the building.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.sunderland.gov.uk/Public/Editable/Themes/Lifelong-Learning/Leaflets/Washington%20Old%20Hall.pdf |title=Sunderland City Council information leaflet |access-date=19 February 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927201653/http://www.sunderland.gov.uk/Public/Editable/Themes/Lifelong-Learning/Leaflets/Washington%20Old%20Hall.pdf |archive-date=27 September 2007 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

As a result of these historic ties, in 2007, [[Washington, D.C.]], and the [[City of Sunderland]] announced a "friendship agreement," hoping to create cultural and economic ties with one another.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/england/wear/6999728.stm|title=Students seal 'friendship' pact|date=17 September 2007|publisher=BBC|access-date=3 December 2020}}</ref>

'''Packwood House''' is a timber-framed [[Tudor style architecture|Tudor]] manor house in [[Packwood, Warwickshire|Packwood]] on the [[Metropolitan Borough of Solihull|Solihull]] border near [[Lapworth]], [[Warwickshire]].  Owned by the [[National Trust]] since 1941,<ref name="handbook" /> the house is a [[Grade I listed building]].<ref>{{NHLE |num=1184240 |desc=Packwood House|grade=I |accessdate=9 March 2015}}</ref> It has a wealth of tapestries and fine furniture, and is known for the garden of [[Taxus baccata|yews]].<ref name="handbook" />

== History ==
The house began as a modest timber-framed farmhouse constructed for John Fetherston between 1556 and 1560. The last member of the Fetherston family died in 1876.<ref name="gardens">{{harvtxt|Gateway Gardens Trust|2007|p=9}}</ref>  In 1904 the house was purchased by [[Birmingham]] industrialist Alfred Ash.<ref name="touruk">{{harvtxt|TourUK|2009}}</ref> It was inherited by Graham Baron Ash (Baron in this case being a name not a title) in 1925,<ref name="gardens" /> who spent the following two decades creating a house of Tudor character. He purchased an extensive collection of 16th- and 17th-century furniture, some obtained from nearby [[Baddesley Clinton]]. The great barn of the farm was converted into a Tudor-style hall with [[sprung floor]] for dancing, and was connected to the main house by the addition of a Long Gallery in 1931.<ref name="staveley">{{harvtxt|Staveley|2009}}</ref>

In 1941, Ash donated the house and gardens to the National Trust in memory of his parents but continued to live in the house until 1947 when he moved to [[Wingfield Castle]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Allesley and Coundon Wedge Conservation Society|2009|p=1}}</ref>

=== Gardens ===
The famous [[Taxus baccata|Yew Garden]] containing over 100 trees was laid out in the mid-17th century by John Fetherston, the lawyer. The clipped yews are supposed to represent "The [[Sermon on the Mount]]". Twelve great yews are known as the "[[Apostles in the New Testament|Apostles]]" and the four big specimens in the middle are 'The [[Four Evangelists|Evangelist]]s'. A tight spiral path lined with box hedges climbs a hummock named "The Mount". The single yew that crowns the summit is known as "The Master". The smaller yew trees are called "The Multitude" and were planted in the 19th century to replace an orchard.<ref name="touruk" />
{{Wide image|PackwoodHouse.JPG|900px||Panoramic view of Packwood House}}

The Yew Garden is entered by raised steps and a wrought-iron gate. The garden path follows an avenue of trees, which leads up a spiral hill<ref name="handbook" /> where a wooden seat is placed beneath a yew tree. This vantage point provides views of the house and the Yew Garden.<ref name="staveley" />

Some of the yews at Packwood are taller than {{convert|50|ft|m}}.<ref name="blagg">{{harvtxt|Blagg|2010}}</ref> The soil on the estate has a high level of clay, which is detrimental to the trees during wet periods. As a result, parts of the garden are often closed to the public while restoration work is undertaken<ref name="blagg" /> The house and gardens are open to the public throughout the whole year as of 2013.<ref>[http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-packwoodhouse Packwood House, National Trust] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111015164700/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-packwoodhouse |date=2011-10-15 }}</ref>
