'''Farnborough Hall''' is a [[country house]] in [[Warwickshire]], [[England]] near to the town of [[Banbury]]. It has been owned by the [[National Trust]] since 1960 when Geoffrey Holbech endowed the house and estate, and is still administered by the Holbech family; the house is a Grade I [[listed building]].

== History ==
Ambrose Holbech acquired the Farnborough estate in 1684 from the Ralegh family, who had owned it since the thirteenth century.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last=Meir |first=Jennifer |date=1997 |title=Sanderson Miller and the Landscaping of Wroxton Abbey, Farnborough Hall and Honington Hall |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1587155 |journal=Garden History |volume=25 |issue=1 |pages=81–106 |doi=10.2307/1587155 |jstor=1587155 |issn=0307-1243|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Archaeological research has demonstrated that the Raleghs had re-sited the hall from its former, moated location earlier in the seventeenth century.<ref name=":1">{{cite journal |last=Wass |first=Stephen |date=2 January 2016 |title=A Way With Water — Water Resources and the Life of an 18th-Century Park |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/03090728.2016.1156849 |journal=Industrial Archaeology Review |volume=38 |issue=1 |pages=59–74 |doi=10.1080/03090728.2016.1156849 |s2cid=163255093 |issn=0309-0728|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The new house was built of [[Cotswolds|Hornton stone]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Delve into the history of Farnborough Hall |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/farnborough-hall/features/delve-into-the-history-of-farnborough-hall |access-date=1 October 2022 |website=National Trust }}</ref> Although it was Ambrose Holbech who had purchased the property, it was his son William who began to renovate it after his marriage to Elizabeth Arlington in 1692.<ref name=":7">{{cite book |title=Farnborough Hall |publisher=National Trust |year=1999 |isbn=9781843590774 |edition=Revised |pages=4, 25}}</ref>

William Holbech inherited the estate, and, after his return from a [[Grand Tour]] in the 1730s, began a scheme of work {{circa|1740}} to make it a suitable setting for the display of the art and antiquities he returned with.<ref name=":2">{{cite web |title=Explore the secrets of Farnborough Hall |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/farnborough-hall/features/things-to-see-and-do-at-farnborough-hall |access-date=1 October 2022 |website=National Trust }}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Scholl |first=Andreas| title=Die antiken Skulpturen in Farnborough Hall sowie in Althorp House, Blenheim Palace, Lyme Park und Penrice Castle |series=Corpus Signorum Imperii Romani Great Britain | volume=3,7 |location=Mainz |publisher=Philipp von Zabern |year=1995 | isbn=3-8053-1738-7}}</ref> His collection included ceramics and sculpture, as well as paintings by [[Canaletto]] and [[Giovanni Paolo Panini]].<ref name=":2" /> The interiors of the house include extremely fine plasterwork undertaken by [[Stucco|stuccatore]] [[William Perritt (stuccatore)|William Perritt]].<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":0" /> The hall was remodelled in the [[Palladian architecture|Palladian style]] {{circa|1745}}–1750, for William Holbech, perhaps by the designer [[Sanderson Miller]].<ref name="listing2"/> Much of what is known about this period comes from a work written by Miller's great-grandson Reverend George Miller, who published a history of Farnborough in his  ''Rambles Round the Edge Hills,'' published in 1900''.<ref name=":0" />'' 

In 1771, another [[William Holbech (MP for Banbury)|William Holbech]] inherited the estate.<ref>{{cite web |title=HOLBECH, William (1748–1812), of Farnborough Hall, Warws. {{!}} History of Parliament Online |url=http://www.historyofparliamentonline.org/volume/1790-1820/member/holbech-william-1748-1812 |access-date=1 October 2022 |website=www.historyofparliamentonline.org}}</ref> Since 2015 the Trust has been working to restore the parkland to the design shown on a surviving estate plan that dates to 1772.<ref name=":4">{{cite web |title=Explore the historic parkland |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/farnborough-hall/features/the-views-and-vistas-of-farnboroughs-historic-parkland |access-date=1 October 2022 |website=National Trust }}</ref> From 1815 to 1816, another Holbech commissioned [[Henry Hakewill]] to build a new coach-house<ref>{{NHLE |desc=FARNBOROUGH HALL COACH HOUSE AND ATTACHED WALL AND GATEPIER, Farnborough  |num=1024458 |access-date=1 October 2022 }}</ref> and remodel the rose garden, and path down to the cascade – referred to today as 'Granny's Walk'. 

During the First World War, the hall was adapted to become a hospital, and was known as Farnborough Auxiliary Hospital.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://www.redcross.org.uk/-/media/documents/about-us/our-history/list-of-auxiliary-hospitals-in-the-uk-during-the-first-world-war.pdf |title=List of auxiliary hospitals in the UK during the First World War |publisher=Red Cross |pages=29 |archive-date=12 August 2022 |access-date=1 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220812145659/https://www.redcross.org.uk/-/media/documents/about-us/our-history/list-of-auxiliary-hospitals-in-the-uk-during-the-first-world-war.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> After the war the originals of the Canaletto and Pannini paintings were sold by Ronald Holbech, although the final publication of the Will of Lieutenant W. H. Holbech, Ronald's older brother, states that "his household effects, etc. at Farnborough Hall, are to devolve as heirlooms with the property as settled on 2nd February 1910. The residue of his property is left equally to his brother, Ronald Acland Holbech, and his sisters Olive Ruth Holbech and Marjory Walrond Holbech."<ref name=":6">{{cite web |title=GIOVANNI ANTONIO CANAL, CALLED CANALETTO (VENICE 1697–1768) |url=https://www.christies.com/en/lot/lot-6387095 |access-date=1 October 2022 |website=www.christies.com }}</ref> For example, one of the paintings by Canaletto that was sold was entitled ''Venice, the Grand Canal looking East with Santa Maria della Salute.<ref name=":6" />''

During the Second World War the house was used as an auxiliary military hospital.<ref name=":7" />
	
The estate was endowed to the National Trust in 1960 by Geoffrey Holbech,<ref name=":3">{{cite web |title=Restoring Farnborough's Historic Parkland – phase 1 |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/farnborough-hall/projects/restoring-farnboroughs-historic-parkland- |access-date=1 October 2022 |website=National Trust }}</ref> after Geoffrey inherited the house and estate from his late older brother at the end of the Second World War. 

As of 2022, Geoffrey Holbech's daughter (Caroline Beddall) and family continued to live in the hall, and administer seasonal visitor access on behalf of the Trust.<ref>{{cite web |title=Farnborough Hall |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/farnborough-hall |access-date=1 October 2022 |website=National Trust }}</ref> 

== Gardens and parkland ==
The parkland is a rare surviving example of the [[ferme ornée]] (ornamental farm) style of landscaping.<ref name=":4" /> It combined agricultural practicality with fashionable design: farm buildings were ornamental, yet suited for their purpose, and could be features within the landscape.<ref name=":5">{{cite web |title=The vision behind Farnborough's parkland |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/farnborough-hall/features/celebrating-300-years-of-sanderson-miller-landscape-designer-of-farnborough-parkland |access-date=1 October 2022 |website=National Trust }}</ref> [[Sanderson Miller]], a contemporary of [[Capability Brown]], remodelled the parkland at the request of William Holbech II.<ref name=":5" />
[[File:Obelisk_at_Farnborough_Hall.jpg|thumb|Obelisk at Farnborough Hall]]
One of the most significant introductions to the garden design was the Terrace Walk, which was constructed on an existing slope and has 26 viewing points along it.<ref name=":5" /> It is 1200m long.<ref name=":1" /> Closest to the Hall is the Game Larder overlooking St Botolph's Church, Farnborough; this is followed by the Ionic Temple and Oval Pavilion.<ref name=":0" /> At the end of the Terrace Walk, is the 18m high Obelisk, which overlooks the [[Warmington, Warwickshire|Warmington]] Valley.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":2" /> The Obelisk was first recorded by a visitor in 1746.<ref name=":0" /> It was rebuilt in 1828 after it collapsed in 1823 and has the names of many visitors etched into the base – most notably one of an Italian [[prisoner of war]] that was inscribed during the [[Second World War]].<ref name="Gardens Trust2">Nicholson, Jean et al: ''The Obelisks of Warwickshire'', page 19. Brewin Books, 2013</ref> The Terrace scheme also included a cascade; repairs to it were undertaken in 2016.<ref>{{cite web |title=Cascade phase 2 complete |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/farnborough-hall/projects/work-begins-on-the-cascade |access-date=1 October 2022 |website=National Trust }}</ref> The park also included a Georgian amphitheatre.<ref name=":1" />

=== Water ===
Miller also introduced a more naturalistic look to the parkland, which included the construction of sinuous pond, known as the Serpentine, designed to look like a river.<ref name=":5" /> Repairs to which were undertaken in 2015.<ref name=":3" /> Miller also engineered part of the River Sor, elevating it 5 metres higher, to form an ornamental pool which could be viewed from the house.<ref name=":5" /> Known as the Oval Pond, this feature had dried out; as of 2016, its outline could still be seen in earthworks.<ref name=":1" /> Above it lay Sourland Pond, which was constructed on land that was already waterlogged.<ref name=":1" />

=== Planting ===
[[File:Farnborough Hall Rose Garden 1.jpg|thumb|Farnborough Hall Rose Garden ]]
Miller used trees, such as [[Pinus sylvestris|Scots pines]], to draw attention to features in the landscape, both close to the house and further away.<ref name=":5" /> In addition, between 1786 and 1790, several [[Cedrus libani|cedar of Lebanon]] trees were given to Mrs William Holbech by her great-grandson Lord Warwick, for the estate.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Hepper |first=F. Nigel |date=1 November 2001 |title=The Cultivation of the Cedar of Lebanon in Western European Parks and Gardens from the 17th to the 19th Century |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/03071375.2001.9747306 |journal=Arboricultural Journal |volume=25 |issue=3 |pages=197–219 |doi=10.1080/03071375.2001.9747306 |s2cid=162191380 |issn=0307-1375|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

The gardens also include the remains of an orangery and a rose garden.<ref name=":2" />

== Legacy ==
The estate and gardens at Farnborough are notable not just for the preservation of the [[ferme ornée]] (ornamental farm) style of landscaping.<ref name=":4" /> They also represent an important stage in the development of the [[English landscape garden]] movement in the first half of the eighteenth century.<ref name=":0" />

It is a Grade I [[listed building]].<ref name="listing2">{{NHLE|num=1374964|desc=Farnborough Hall|accessdate=5 July 2022}}</ref>

== In popular culture ==
The first mention of the landscape garden in literature is found in a poem called ''Edgehill'' by [[Richard Jago]].<ref name=":0" />

Farnborough Hall featured in the 1966 film ''[[Grand Prix (1966 film)|Grand Prix]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0060472/locations/?ref_=tt_dt_loc|title=Grand Prix (1966) - Filming & production - IMDb|accessdate=22 January 2025|via=www.imdb.com}}</ref>
